summary: The note explains the term "baby boom" as a noticeable rise in the birth rate and traces its use, including a 1951 New York Post column by Sylvia F. Porter describing post-war population growth. It notes the first recorded use of "baby boomer" in a 1970 Washington Post article. It also shows that authors define the boom generation's dates differently, citing Landon Jones (1943 to 1960) and William Strauss and Neil Howe (1943 to 1960).
one_line: Overview of the post-war "baby boom" term and the differing date ranges authors use to define the Baby Boomer generation.
key_facts: The phrase "baby boom" refers to a noticeable increase in the birth rate.
Sylvia F. Porter used the word "boom" to describe the post-war population increase in a column for the May 4, 1951, edition of the New York Post.
The column was based on a U.S. population increase of 2,357,000 in 1950.
According to the Oxford English Dictionary, the first recorded use of "baby boomer" is from 1970 in an article in The Washington Post.
Various authors have delimited the baby boom period differently.
Landon Jones, in his book Great Expectations: America and the Baby Boom Generation (1980), defined the baby-boom generation as extending from 1943 through 1960.
Landon Jones defined the span of the baby-boom generation as the years when annual births increased over 4,000,000.
William Strauss and Neil Howe, known for their generational theory, define the social generation of Boomers as those born from 1943 to 1960.
Strauss and Howe describe Boomers as too young to have any personal memory of World War II but old enough to remember the postwar American High.
